title: Robot manipulation is two to three orders of magnitude harder than motion control, and Silicon Valley has bet the wrong way
dek: Sudo believes the mainstream Silicon Valley end-to-end imitation learning route has a fundamental flaw in open-world manipulation, and that a hierarchical top-down/bottom-up structure will return to the mainstream in the second half of this year.
why: This episode is information-dense, suited to founders and investors who want to understand the divergence in embodied AI technical routes, the feasibility of Sim2Real, and the landscape of Silicon Valley robotics companies.
who: Founders, investors and robotics engineers following the divergence in embodied AI technical routes, especially those who want to understand Sim2Real feasibility, data cold-start strategies and the Silicon Valley competitive landscape.
skip: The discussion from 1:09:01 to 1:10:58 about Amazon and vertical-scenario commercialization, which is low in information density.

points.h: Video training cannot reach sub-millimeter precision
points.body: Han Zheng explains why you cannot directly train robot manipulation on internet video. 2D images and video do contain three-dimensional information, but it is "not quite complete, and not quite accurate." Autonomous driving navigation only needs precision of around 10 centimeters, but robot manipulation demands sub-millimeter precision — for example, inserting a cable into the corresponding hole. Only datasets built from 3D modeling can achieve that precision. The simulator requires the robot's understanding of geometric precision to reach millimeter or even sub-millimeter level.

points.h: Zero-shot general grasping hits 98% single-attempt success
points.body: In internal tests in November and December last year, Sudo R1 operated over 100 objects for a continuous hour, 240 pick-and-place cycles, and none of these objects had ever appeared in the training data. Single-attempt pick-and-place success rate was close to 98%, and if the first attempt failed, the robot would use closed-loop control to rapidly adjust its strategy and reach 100%. Han Zheng calls this the first time the Sim2Real route has closed the gap. Afterwards they had nearly 1,000 people test it with random objects on site at ICRA and CVPR, something no one had done at academic conferences before.

points.h: Short-skill generalization matters more than chaining long-horizon tasks
points.body: Han Zheng argues that zero-shot stable short skills for manipulating basic objects in the open world are more core than reproducing long-horizon tasks. If short skills are stable and reliable enough, with sufficiently high generalization, they can be assembled into all kinds of long-horizon operations. This is also the core idea of the ManiSkill framework. Around the same time the Sudo team proposed chain of thought in 2023, there was a piece of work called Chain of Thought Predictive Control, specifically addressing the chaining of short tasks into long-horizon tasks.

points.h: Manipulating objects is two to three orders of magnitude harder than motion control
points.body: Han Zheng points out that reinforcement learning in simulation and Sim2Real have already been fully validated in motion control for Boston Dynamics and Unitree humanoid robots and quadruped dogs, and part of the reinforcement learning engine inside Nvidia Isaac was contributed early on by members of the Sudo team. But when a robot manipulates objects, the difficulty is two to three orders of magnitude higher. Because motion control only needs to focus on its own actions, it does not need to understand object shape or material, nor does it need to know how to move near an object and make adjustments.

points.h: Tesla cannot be replicated; cold start must rely on simulation
points.body: Han Zheng explains why robots cannot collect data by selling cars the way Tesla did. Tesla started selling cars over a decade ago, millions of drivers drive on the road every day, and data accumulates naturally. But it is very hard for a robot to sell 5 million units into offices and homes before it has any function, with a worker standing next to it remote-controlling it. Domestic companies might reach a scale of a hundred or even a thousand units, but that is far from 5 million or 10 million units entering every household. So the cold start must rely on simulation, requiring millions or even tens of millions of full data collected in open environments.

points.h: The hierarchical structure Silicon Valley abandoned is about to return to the mainstream
points.body: Han Zheng reveals that when Physical Intelligence was still at Google Robotics before it was founded, everyone tacitly assumed that once the low-level model had stable manipulation capability, the high level would handle environment understanding and task decomposition. But when they founded their startups in 2023 and 2024, everyone chose the end-to-end playbook they were good at and familiar with, and stopped mentioning hierarchy. Han Zheng's hot take is: starting in the second half of this year, the hierarchical top-down/bottom-up structure will return to the mainstream, and may be the final commercialization solution. After exchanges between academia and industry in recent weeks, some people have already realized this could be the new direction.

points.h: Most bullish on DeepMind plus Boston Dynamics Atlas
points.body: Han Zheng considers the biggest competitor to be DeepMind plus the electric version of Boston Dynamics Atlas. Last year's Demis Hassabis interviews and documentary showed that Google's bet on physical-world AI is the most resolute among all the big companies. They have already switched their hardware platform from Apptronik to the electric version of Atlas, and poached core people from Boston Dynamics' hardware division to DeepMind. Google also acquired the MuJoCo team, has its own world model Genie 3, and has almost unlimited GPUs and the best talent. Han Zheng believes this is simply not on the same order of magnitude as other companies.

points.h: Amazon has many scenarios but integration is difficult
points.body: Han Zheng believes Amazon has always been the big company investing the most in robotics, with warehousing and logistics AGVs, Kiva, various robotic arms and humanoid robot companies such as Agility and Covariant. It will provide scenarios, but in the end it will either acquire these companies or do it itself. Covariant at the time also counted Amazon as one of its core customers. But integrating multiple robot systems is difficult.
